title: CPR / Cardiac Arrest
short_description: Immediate life-support procedure for someone who is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
warning: CRITICAL EMERGENCY: Cardiac arrest requires immediate CPR and urgent emergency services dispatch.
steps: Check the scene for safety and ensure you are not in danger.
Check for responsiveness: Tap the person's shoulders firmly and shout 'Are you okay?'.
Call 112 (or local emergency services) immediately or instruct someone nearby to call and fetch an AED.
Check breathing for 10 seconds: If not breathing or only gasping, position the person on their back on a firm surface.
Place your hands in the center of the chest (lower half of breastbone). Interlock your fingers.
Push hard and fast: Perform compressions at a rate of 100–120 beats per minute, at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep. Allow full chest recoil.
If trained, deliver 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions. Otherwise, perform hands-only CPR continuously.
Continue compressions until the person shows signs of life, an AED arrives, or emergency paramedics take over.
when_to_call_emergency: Person is unresponsive and not breathing normally or gasping
Sudden collapse without warning
No detectable pulse or signs of circulation
do_not_list: Do not delay starting CPR to look for a pulse if untrained
Do not perform CPR on a conscious or normally breathing person
Do not interrupt compressions for more than 10 seconds

title: Choking
short_description: Emergency protocol for severe airway blockage in an adult or child.
warning: Act immediately if the person cannot breathe, speak, or cough effectively.
steps: Assess severity: Ask 'Are you choking?'. If they can speak or cough loudly, encourage them to keep coughing.
If they cannot breathe, speak, or cough, call emergency services (112) immediately.
Stand behind the person, lean them slightly forward, and give up to 5 firm back blows between their shoulder blades using the heel of your hand.
If back blows fail, perform abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver): Stand behind, wrap arms around waist, place fist just above navel.
Grasp your fist with your other hand and pull inward and upward sharply up to 5 times.
Alternate between 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until object is dislodged or person becomes unresponsive.
If person becomes unresponsive, lower them to the floor safely and begin CPR compressions immediately.
when_to_call_emergency: Person cannot breathe, turn blue, or lose consciousness
Airway remains blocked after 5 back blows and abdominal thrusts
Person becomes unresponsive
do_not_list: Do not perform blind finger sweeps in the mouth
Do not perform abdominal thrusts on infants under 1 year (use back blows and chest thrusts instead)
Do not slap a choking person if they are coughing effectively

title: Severe Bleeding
short_description: Urgent control of major hemorrhaging to prevent hemorrhagic shock.
warning: Uncontrolled severe bleeding can be life-threatening within minutes. Call 112 immediately.
steps: Ensure area safety and put on protective gloves if available.
Call 112 (or emergency services) immediately for uncontrollable or spurting bleeding.
Expose the wound by removing or cutting away clothing to locate the exact source of bleeding.
Apply direct, continuous pressure over the wound using a clean cloth, sterile bandage, or gloved hands.
Maintain firm pressure without releasing to check the wound for at least 5-10 minutes.
If blood soaks through, do not remove the original dressing; add more layers on top and compress harder.
If bleeding is on a limb and direct pressure fails to control severe arterial bleeding, apply a commercial tourniquet 2-3 inches above the wound.
Keep the person warm, lying down, and quiet to treat for shock until paramedics arrive.
when_to_call_emergency: Bleeding is spurting, heavy, or does not stop after 10 minutes of direct pressure
Wound is deep, exposes muscle/bone, or contains embedded objects
Person shows signs of shock (pale skin, confusion, rapid weak pulse)
do_not_list: Do not remove embedded objects from the wound; pad around them
Do not remove blood-soaked bandages—apply new dressings over them
Do not apply tourniquets over joints or use thin wire/string as a makeshift tourniquet

title: Burns
short_description: First-aid guidance for heat, chemical, or electrical burn injuries.
warning: Seek urgent medical attention for severe, extensive, facial, or chemical/electrical burns.
steps: Ensure your own safety and stop the burning process immediately (extinguish flames, disconnect power).
Cool the burn: Hold the affected area under cool running tap water for 10 to 20 minutes. Do not use ice water.
Remove jewelry, watches, or non-sticking clothing near the burned area before swelling occurs.
Cover the burn loosely with a sterile, non-adherent bandage or clean plastic cling wrap to prevent infection.
Keep the person warm with a blanket over uninjured areas to prevent hypothermia.
Administer over-the-counter pain relievers if appropriate and person is conscious.
Seek emergency medical assistance (112) for severe, large, or facial burns.
when_to_call_emergency: Burn covers a large area (larger than person's palm)
Burn is deep, charred, white, or leathery (3rd degree)
Burn involves face, hands, feet, groin, major joints, or airway
Burn is caused by chemicals, high-voltage electricity, or explosion
do_not_list: Do not apply ice, ice water, butter, oil, toothpaste, or ointments to open burns
Do not pop blisters or peel away burned skin
Do not remove clothing stuck to burned skin

title: Fractures & Bone Injuries
short_description: Care for suspected broken bones, dislocations, or major joint trauma.
warning: Immobilize the limb. Do not attempt to realign or push back protruding bones.
steps: Keep the person still and calm. Avoid moving them unless immediate physical danger exists.
Call 112 immediately if open fracture (bone protruding), severe pain, or spine/neck injury is suspected.
Control any visible bleeding around the injury site by pressing gently around protruding bone.
Immobilize the injured area in the position found using a splint or padding (newspaper, cardboard, cloth).
Apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth to reduce swelling and pain for 15-20 minutes.
Treat for shock: Keep the person lying flat and covered with a warm blanket.
Monitor circulation below the injury site (check warmth, feeling, and skin color).
when_to_call_emergency: Bone is piercing through the skin (open fracture)
Injured limb appears deformed, crooked, or lacks sensation/pulse
Head, neck, or back spinal injury is suspected
Person cannot bear weight or is in excruciating pain
do_not_list: Do not try to force or push a broken bone back into place
Do not test ability to walk or move an injured joint
Do not move a person with suspected spine or neck trauma

title: Fainting (Syncope)
short_description: Response for temporary loss of consciousness due to reduced brain blood flow.
warning: If fainting lasts longer than 1 minute or occurs with chest pain, call emergency services.
steps: Position the person safely: Lie them flat on their back on the floor.
Elevate their legs about 12 inches (30 cm) above heart level to restore blood flow to the brain.
Loosen tight clothing around the neck, chest, and waist (collars, belts).
Ensure adequate ventilation: Open windows or clear crowding people away.
Check responsiveness and breathing: Ensure airway is open and clear.
If the person recovers, keep them lying down for several minutes before helping them sit up slowly.
If they do not regain consciousness within 1 minute, call 112 and prepare to perform CPR if breathing stops.
when_to_call_emergency: Person remains unconscious for more than 60 seconds
Fainting is accompanied by chest pain, shortness of breath, or numbness
Person suffered a head injury during the fall
Person has a history of heart conditions or diabetes
do_not_list: Do not splash cold water on their face or slap them
Do not give food, water, or medicine until fully alert and standing stably
Do not stand the person up quickly immediately after regaining consciousness

title: Seizures & Convulsions
short_description: First-aid for epileptic fits, seizures, or sudden involuntary jerking movements.
warning: Protect the person from harm. Never place objects inside their mouth.
steps: Stay calm and note the exact start time of the seizure.
Protect from injury: Clear sharp or hard objects away from the surrounding area.
Cushion their head with a folded jacket, towel, or soft pillow.
Do not hold them down or restrain their movements.
Gently roll the person onto their side (recovery position) as soon as shaking stops to keep airway clear.
Reassure the person as they regain consciousness, as they may feel confused or tired.
Time the duration: Call 112 if the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes or repeats.
when_to_call_emergency: Seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes
Second seizure follows immediately without regaining consciousness
Person is pregnant, diabetic, or injured during the fall
Seizure occurs in water or person has difficulty breathing afterwards
do_not_list: Do not put anything in the person's mouth (no spoon, wallet, or fingers)
Do not try to restrain, hold down, or stop their jerking movements
Do not offer water or food until they are completely alert

title: Electric Shock
short_description: High and low voltage electrical contact safety and resuscitation protocol.
warning: DO NOT touch a victim who is still in contact with an active electric source.
steps: Ensure safety first: Do NOT touch the person if they are still touching the live electrical source.
Turn off the main power breaker/switch immediately, or unplug the appliance safely.
If power cannot be cut, use a non-conductive object (dry wooden broomstick or rubber mat) to push the source away.
Call 112 immediately for emergency medical assistance.
Once safe, check for breathing and responsiveness.
If the person is not breathing, start CPR compressions hard and fast immediately.
Treat visible electrical burns with cool water and cover loosely with sterile dry dressings.
when_to_call_emergency: All high-voltage electrical injuries require emergency hospital evaluation
Person experienced loss of consciousness, confusion, or difficulty breathing
Person exhibits irregular heart rate, burns, or muscle pain
do_not_list: Do not touch the victim with bare hands while electrical current is active
Do not go near high-voltage wires until power company confirms shut-off
Do not apply ice or butter to electrical burn entry/exit wounds

title: Poisoning & Ingestion
short_description: Action guide for toxic substance ingestion, chemical inhalation, or overdose.
warning: Identify the toxic substance if safe. Do not induce vomiting unless advised by medical professionals.
steps: Ensure scene safety and remove the person from toxic fumes or chemical source if applicable.
Check responsiveness and breathing. Call 112 or local Poison Control immediately.
If poison was swallowed: Do NOT induce vomiting unless specifically instructed by poison control experts.
If toxic fumes inhaled: Move person to fresh outdoor air immediately.
If chemical on skin/eyes: Flush continuously with clean tepid water for at least 15-20 minutes.
Save the chemical container, bottle, or plant sample for medical personnel identification.
If person loses consciousness or stops breathing, place flat and start CPR.
when_to_call_emergency: Person is confused, drowsy, vomiting, or losing consciousness
Hazardous chemical, acid, detergent, or drug overdose suspected
Difficulty breathing or chest tightness present
do_not_list: Do not induce vomiting unless explicitly directed by Poison Control or medical doctors
Do not give syrup of ipecac, salt water, or charcoal on your own
Do not neutralize acids with alkalis or give drink to an unconscious person

title: Heat Stroke & Hyperthermia
short_description: Emergency cooling protocol for severe heat-related illness and high body temperature.
warning: Heat stroke is a medical emergency that can damage internal organs. Rapid cooling is crucial.
steps: Call 112 immediately if person has high temperature (>103°F/40°C), confusion, or altered mental state.
Move the person to a cool, shaded, or air-conditioned indoor area immediately.
Remove heavy outer clothing and loosen tight garments.
Rapidly cool the body: Apply cool wet towels, sponge skin with water, or place ice packs under armpits, neck, and groin.
Fan the person continuously while keeping skin moist to promote evaporative cooling.
If conscious and able to swallow, offer small sips of cool water or electrolyte drink.
Monitor temperature and breathing until emergency responders arrive.
when_to_call_emergency: Core body temperature elevated with hot, red, dry, or damp skin
Confusion, slurred speech, delirium, or loss of consciousness
Vomiting or inability to drink fluids
do_not_list: Do not give ice-cold water to drink rapidly
Do not give aspirin or acetaminophen for heat stroke temperature
Do not leave the person unattended in hot surroundings

title: Nosebleed (Epistaxis)
short_description: First-aid steps to stop nasal bleeding efficiently and prevent blood swallowing.
warning: Sit upright and lean forward slightly. Do not tilt head back.
steps: Sit upright and lean your head and torso slightly forward to prevent blood flowing down your throat.
Pinch the soft lower part of your nose firmly between your thumb and index finger.
Breathe through your mouth while maintaining continuous pinch pressure for 10 to 15 minutes.
Apply a cold compress or ice pack wrapped in cloth across the bridge of your nose.
Do not release pinch pressure early to check if bleeding has stopped until 10 full minutes pass.
Spit out any blood that collects in your mouth rather than swallowing it.
If bleeding persists after 20 minutes of continuous pressure, seek emergency care.
when_to_call_emergency: Bleeding continues for longer than 20 minutes despite continuous pressure
Nosebleed occurs after severe head injury or facial trauma
Person feels lightheaded, dizzy, or bleeds excessively
do_not_list: Do not tilt your head backward (this causes blood to drain into stomach and lungs)
Do not pack nasal cavity with tissue paper or cotton wool balls
Do not blow nose or lie flat immediately after bleeding stops

title: Severe Allergic Reaction (Anaphylaxis)
short_description: Rapid intervention for anaphylactic shock caused by food, stings, or medication.
warning: ANAPHYLAXIS IS LIFE-THREATENING. Administer epinephrine (EpiPen) immediately if available and call 112.
steps: Call 112 immediately for emergency medical assistance at the first sign of severe reaction.
Check if the person carries an Epinephrine Auto-Injector (EpiPen). Help them administer it into the outer thigh.
Position the person lying flat on their back. If breathing is difficult, allow them to sit up slightly.
Loosen tight clothing around neck and chest.
Remove allergen source if safe (e.g., scrape away bee stinger gently with a card).
Keep person warm and quiet. Do not give anything to drink.
If breathing stops or person becomes unresponsive, start CPR compressions immediately.
when_to_call_emergency: Swelling of lips, tongue, throat, or face
Wheezing, severe shortness of breath, or gasping
Hives spreading rapidly across body with dizziness or fainting
do_not_list: Do not delay using an epinephrine auto-injector if anaphylaxis symptoms appear
Do not force an anaphylactic person to walk or stand up suddenly
Do not give oral allergy pills if person has trouble breathing or swallowing

title: Sprains & Strains
short_description: R.I.C.E. protocol for ligament sprains and muscle strain injuries.
warning: Apply the R.I.C.E protocol (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) for joint sprains.
steps: Rest: Stop activity immediately and avoid putting weight on the injured limb or joint.
Ice: Apply an ice pack wrapped in a damp towel for 15-20 minutes every 2-3 hours.
Compression: Wrap the area firmly with an elastic crepe bandage to control swelling (do not wrap too tightly).
Elevation: Prop the injured joint above heart level using pillows to reduce fluid accumulation.
Avoid H.A.R.M. in first 48 hours: Heat, Alcohol, Running, and Massage.
Over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen can help manage discomfort if tolerated.
Seek medical evaluation if unable to bear weight or joint is unstable.
when_to_call_emergency: Inability to bear any weight on the joint or severe immobility
Numbness, tingling, or cold feeling in toes/fingers below injury
Visible deformity or severe bruising indicating possible fracture
do_not_list: Do not apply direct heat or hot baths in the first 48 hours
Do not force movement or stretch an acutely sprained joint
Do not wrap compression bandage so tight that it cuts off blood circulation

title: Minor Cuts & Minor Wounds
short_description: Clean, disinfect, and dress superficial lacerations, scrapes, and minor cuts.
warning: Clean thoroughly to prevent tetanus and bacterial wound infection.
steps: Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water before touching the wound.
Apply gentle direct pressure with a sterile gauze pad to stop minor oozing.
Rinse the wound thoroughly under cool running tap water for 5 minutes to remove dirt and debris.
Clean skin around the wound with mild soap and water; avoid getting soap directly in open cut.
Apply a thin layer of over-the-counter antiseptic cream or ointment if available.
Cover the cut with a sterile adhesive bandage (plaster) or sterile dressing.
Change dressing daily or whenever it becomes wet or dirty, and check for signs of infection.
when_to_call_emergency: Cut is deep, gaping open, or requires stitches
Wound was caused by rusty metal, animal bite, or dirty object (tetanus risk)
Redness, heat, pus, or fever develops (signs of infection)
do_not_list: Do not scrub deep or dirty wounds harshly
Do not use hydrogen peroxide or rubbing alcohol directly inside fresh open cuts
Do not blow on an open wound with your mouth

title: Medical Shock
short_description: Emergency stabilization for medical shock (insufficient blood flow to tissues).
warning: CRITICAL: Medical shock is a life-threatening state requiring urgent emergency paramedics.
steps: Call 112 immediately—medical shock is a life-threatening medical emergency.
Lay the person down flat on their back safely.
Elevate their legs about 12 inches (30 cm) unless spinal, head, or leg injury is suspected.
Keep the person still and calm. Loosen tight clothing around neck and waist.
Keep them warm: Cover them with a blanket or coat to preserve body heat.
Do NOT give them food or water, even if they complain of thirst.
Monitor breathing and pulse continuously until emergency responders arrive; be prepared for CPR.
when_to_call_emergency: Pale, cold, clammy skin with rapid shallow breathing
Weak rapid pulse, confusion, bluish lips or fingernails
Severe blood loss, severe trauma, or severe allergic reaction
do_not_list: Do not give the person anything to eat or drink (risk of aspiration)
Do not elevate legs if you suspect head, neck, back, or leg fracture
Do not move the person unnecessarily

title: Headache & Migraine
short_description: First-aid evaluation and relief guidance for headaches and migraines.
warning: Seek emergency care immediately for sudden 'thunderclap' headache, fever with stiff neck, or confusion.
steps: Assess severity: Sudden severe pain or fever with stiff neck requires emergency call 112.
Rest in a quiet, dark, well-ventilated room with eyes closed.
Apply a cold compress across your forehead or back of neck for relief.
Sip water slowly to stay hydrated.
Avoid bright screens, loud noises, and strong odors.
Take over-the-counter or prescribed migraine medication early if appropriate.
when_to_call_emergency: Sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache reaching peak intensity in seconds
Headache accompanied by stiff neck, high fever, or confusion
Headache with numbness, weakness, or trouble speaking
do_not_list: Do not ignore a sudden severe unmanageable headache
Do not expose eyes to bright screens or harsh lights during migraine attack

title: Nausea & Vomiting
short_description: First-aid guidance for nausea, vomiting, motion sickness, and food poisoning.
warning: Urgent emergency medical care is needed if vomiting blood or dark coffee-ground material.
steps: If vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, call 112 immediately.
Keep person sitting upright or leaning forward to prevent choking/aspiration.
Rest stomach for 1-2 hours after vomiting.
Sip small amounts (teaspoonfuls) of Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) or electrolyte water every 5-10 minutes.
Gradually reintroduce bland foods (Bananas, Rice, Applesauce, Toast).
Avoid solid foods, dairy, caffeine, alcohol, and spicy/fatty meals.
when_to_call_emergency: Vomiting blood or material resembling dark coffee grounds
Inability to keep liquids down for more than 24 hours
Signs of severe dehydration (extreme thirst, dry mouth, no urination, confusion)
do_not_list: Do not give large gulps of water quickly—it triggers reflex vomiting
Do not force person to eat solid food while nauseous

title: Fever & Chills
short_description: Management and first-aid steps for elevated body temperature and chills.
warning: Call 112 immediately if fever is accompanied by stiff neck, confusion, or purple/red rash.
steps: Assess for emergency red flags (stiff neck, confusion, unexplained rash). Call 112 if present.
Rest in a cool, well-ventilated room with lightweight clothing and light blankets.
Drink plenty of water, clear broth, or electrolyte solutions to prevent dehydration.
Apply lukewarm damp cloths to forehead, neck, and wrists.
Take fever-reducing medication (paracetamol or ibuprofen) as directed if needed.
when_to_call_emergency: Fever with stiff neck, severe headache, confusion, or purple rash
Fever exceeding 104°F (40°C) not coming down with fever reducers
Fever lasting more than 3 consecutive days
do_not_list: Do not use ice-cold baths or alcohol rubs to cool down (can trigger shivers and internal temp spike)
Do not bundle up in heavy blankets when shivering with fever

title: Abdominal & Stomach Pain
short_description: First-aid guidance for stomach ache, cramping, gastritis, and appendicitis signs.
warning: Call 112 or visit ER immediately for severe lower right pain, rigid stomach, or vomiting blood.
steps: Assess location and intensity: Lower right abdominal pain with fever suggests appendicitis emergency.
Lie down in a comfortable position (knees slightly bent up can reduce tension).
Apply warm heating pad to abdomen for mild gas or menstrual cramps.
Sip warm chamomile or peppermint tea for mild indigestion.
Avoid eating solid, spicy, or heavy foods until pain subsides.
when_to_call_emergency: Severe lower right abdominal pain with fever or vomiting (suspected appendicitis)
Sudden unbearable severe abdominal pain with sweating or fainting
Abdomen feels hard, rigid, or extremely tender to touch
do_not_list: Do not give food, laxatives, or strong painkillers if appendicitis is suspected
Do not apply direct intense heat over suspected appendicitis

title: Dizziness & Vertigo
short_description: First-aid evaluation for dizziness, lightheadedness, and room-spinning vertigo.
warning: Call 112 immediately if dizziness occurs with facial drooping, arm weakness, or speech difficulty (Stroke FAST).
steps: Check for stroke signs (FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty). Call 112 if present.
Sit down immediately or lie flat on a stable surface to prevent falls.
Keep head still and focus on a fixed point if experiencing room-spinning vertigo.
Sip water or electrolyte fluids slowly if lightheaded from heat or dehydration.
Stand up very slowly when feeling better.
when_to_call_emergency: Dizziness with facial drooping, arm weakness, or slurred speech (Stroke)
Dizziness accompanied by chest pain or fainting
Dizziness following head trauma
do_not_list: Do not try to walk around while feeling dizzy or experiencing vertigo
Do not make sudden head or posture changes

title: Hand & Arm Pain
short_description: First-aid guidance and assessment for hand, wrist, finger, and arm pain.
warning: Seek emergency care immediately if arm pain occurs with chest tightness, or if there is a visible open bone fracture.
steps: Check for emergency red flags (chest tightness/sweating or open fracture). Call 112 if present.
Immobilize and support the injured hand/arm with a cushion, pillow, or sling.
Apply a cold compress wrapped in a cloth for 15-20 minutes to reduce swelling.
Elevate hand above heart level if swelling occurs.
Rest from repetitive tasks (typing, heavy lifting, sports).
when_to_call_emergency: Sudden arm pain with chest pressure, breathlessness, or sweating (Heart Attack warning)
Bone protruding through skin or severe uncontrollable bleeding
Visibly deformed bone or complete inability to move fingers/wrist
do_not_list: Do not try to forcefully straighten or realign a deformed bone or dislodged finger
Do not apply ice directly to bare skin

title: Leg & Foot Pain Guidance
short_description: Evaluation and first-aid for leg, foot, knee, calf, or ankle pain.
warning: Inability to bear weight after trauma or sudden severe swelling with warmth/redness requires urgent medical evaluation.
steps: Rest the affected leg and avoid putting weight on it.
Apply ice packs wrapped in cloth for 15-20 minutes to reduce acute swelling.
Wrap ankle or leg with an elastic bandage for compression.
Elevate leg above heart level when lying down.
If severe pain or inability to walk persists, seek medical evaluation.
when_to_call_emergency: Inability to bear any weight after a fall or high-impact trauma
Visible bone deformity, open wound, or severe numbness
Sudden deep leg swelling accompanied by warmth and redness (suspected DVT)
do_not_list: Do NOT force walking on a severely injured leg
Do NOT apply direct ice on bare skin
Do NOT attempt to realign or pop deformed bones back in place

title: Joint & Back Pain Care
short_description: First-aid care for acute back strain, spinal discomfort, and joint swelling.
warning: Back pain with numbness in legs, loss of bowel/bladder control, or following high-impact trauma requires emergency medical attention.
steps: Rest in a comfortable position, such as lying flat with knees elevated by pillows.
Apply ice to acute joint injuries or heat to muscle spasms after 48 hours.
Avoid heavy lifting, twisting, or sudden bending.
Seek medical evaluation if pain radiates or persists.
when_to_call_emergency: Loss of sensation or numbness in legs or groin
Inability to control bowel or bladder function
Back pain following a major car accident, fall from height, or severe impact
do_not_list: Do NOT move a person with suspected spinal injury
Do NOT lift heavy objects during acute back pain flare-ups
